newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto launches huge pulp mill.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto launches huge pulp mill.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto inaugurated Southeast Asia's largest single-line pulp mill on Wednesday, calling the $1.3 billion project in East Kalimantan province environmentally sustainable.
"The most important thing is we have implemented sustainable development and sustainable biodiversity in Indonesia's forests," Suharto said while inaugurating the PT Kiani Kertas mill.
The mill will start commercial production next week and reach full capacity of 500,000 tonnes of air-dried pulp per annum within three months.

Located on more than 3,400 hectares (8,400 acres) in the heart of thick forests on Indonesia's half of Borneo island, Kiani Kertas is almost completely owned by Indonesian timber king Muhammad "Bob" Hasan through his Kalimanis conglomerate. Kalimanis means Sweet River in the Indonesian language.
Hasan, a close associate of Suharto, told reporters on Tuesday that some of the equity in the mill was held by two charitable foundations headed by the president.
He also said the company would consider floating part of its equity after production was up and running.

Hasan has provided some $700 million of the financing for the project with the rest coming from two bank syndicates. Company officials said the mill took 30 months to construct and that special pains had been taken to maintain the region's ecological balance.

A special conservation area of 34,000 hectares (84,000 acres) within the firm's 450,000 hectares (1.1 million acres) of timber concessions would be protected, allowing wildlife and natural vegetation to be maintained, they said.
Green belts, where no logging will be allowed, will surround the areas that are designated for timber cultivation, they added.
"We have spent $25 million on the conservation area," Hasan said, adding that a huge reforestation programme would be undertaken alongside the logging. "Everything we do here is sustainable."

The mill, located on the Pantai river in a remote area of East Kalimantan, has an airstrip and a river port. Accommodation for some 1,000 employees has been built, and education and health services are planned.

Dick Youngberg, Kiani Kertas' head of marketing, said all the produce of the company would be exported and that some pre-sale contracts had already been signed. Other officials said markets would primarily be in Japan and Taiwan and that export earnings would reach about $225 million per year.
The calculations indicate an average price of about $500 per tonne, which pulp analysts have said is a current fair value although prices are seen rising over the next year or so.
Pulp is a cyclical industry and prices plunged to an average of about $400 per tonne in the first quarter of this year from a peak of $870 in 1995.
"Pulp is now in resurgence," Youngberg said. "In the next nine to 12 months, we look forward to a gradual increase in prices. We've got a well-sold position."
